newsitem.title: FRANCE: French voters cool to Chirac's reassurances.
newsitem.headline: French voters cool to Chirac's reassurances.

text.p: An opposition leader ripped into President Jacques Chirac on Friday for promising a gloomy France more of the same painful austerity while a poll found most voters unmoved by his marathon televised appeal for support.
"I found the president out of touch with the country's realities and the French people's expectations," opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said.

"I wondered whether the people would again elect Jacques Chirac as president, and here he was in a sort of reversal, of roles, telling us, "I have no desire to vote for the French people, such as they are,'" Jospin said on France 2 television.

An instant poll for the left-leaning daily Liberation found that nearly six in 10 adults were unconvinced by Chirac's two-hour television appearance while 54 percent wanted him to dump Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whom he insisted on keeping.

Nineteen months into his seven-year term, the conservative Chirac told voters on Thursday night the country needed more "draconian" budget cuts to restore its finances and join the single European currency before it could revive the economy and curb record unemployment.
The 64-year-old Gaullist ruled out dismissing his prime minister and blamed discontent on a conservative society fearful of the future and paralysed by traditions and corporatism.
He also ruled out a devaluation of the franc suggested by government allies to revive growth and said the euro was vital to give Europe the power to challenge U.S. "hegemony".
Predictably his supporters hailed his courage for sticking to his line despite the government's record unpopularity while his foes accused him of doggedly ignoring failure.
Chirac "stuck to a policy that doesn't work," said Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande.
Juppe, buoyed by Chirac's renewed support, said the president had expressed "a great ambition for a strong, generous and united France".

Analysts had speculated that Chirac would go for a cabinet reshuffle or an early election and voiced disappointment that he had no major announcement in the long-awaited interview, his first major public statement in five months.
"Is that all?" asked Liberation, summing up a general feeling in the press that Chirac had no miracle cure for the country's woes.
The pro-government Le Figaro wrote Chirac had given his rule a "second wind" but the tabloid Le Parisien called the interview, watched live by more than nine million viewers, "The Big Flop".
Chirac's only new announcement was that he was setting up a commission to reform the judiciary by making state prosecutors independent from the Justice Ministry.
The Magistrates' Union welcomed the plan, which followed charges that the government had ordered prosecutors to drop embarrassing political sleaze probes into close allies of Chirac.

Grilled at length on the probes for the first time since he came to office, Chirac said they must be carried out to the end and "punishment must be all the more exemplary as it concerns people in positions of power."
